questions.question: How many carpal bones make up the wrist, and in how many rows are they arranged?
questions.explanation: The carpus is made up of 8 carpal bones arranged in two rows of four: a proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetral, pisiform, from lateral to medial) and a distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate).
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones

questions.question: A fall on the outstretched hand causing tenderness in the anatomical snuff box most classically suggests a fracture of which carpal bone?
questions.explanation: Scaphoid fracture is common after a fall on the outstretched hand and classically presents with tenderness and swelling in the anatomical snuff box, plus pain on longitudinal percussion of the thumb and index finger.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones, Clinical Anatomy

questions.question: Why is a scaphoid fracture through the waist of the bone at particular risk of avascular necrosis?

options.A: The scaphoid has no nutrient artery at all
options.B: Both nutrient arteries typically enter through the distal part (tubercle/body), so a waist fracture can cut off blood supply to the proximal fragment
options.C: The scaphoid is the only carpal bone with no cartilage covering
options.D: Scaphoid fractures always damage the ulnar nerve directly

questions.explanation: The scaphoid's blood supply normally enters via nutrient arteries at the tubercle (palmar surface) and the dorsal surface of the body — both relatively distal. A waist fracture can therefore deprive the proximal fragment of its blood supply, since retrograde flow to that fragment is often insufficient, leading to avascular necrosis and a high risk of nonunion.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones, Clinical Anatomy

questions.question: The lateral surface of the pisiform bone is grooved by which structure?

options.D: The tendon of flexor carpi radialis

questions.explanation: The lateral surface of the pisiform is grooved by the ulnar nerve as it passes into the hand through Guyon's canal, alongside the ulnar artery.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones

questions.question: Dislocation of the lunate bone (from a fall on the acutely dorsiflexed hand) typically displaces it in which direction, and can mimic the features of which condition?

options.A: Displaces posteriorly; mimics De Quervain's tenosynovitis
options.B: Displaces anteriorly; can produce carpal tunnel syndrome-like features
options.C: Displaces laterally; mimics ulnar nerve palsy at the elbow
options.D: Does not displace, only rotates in place with no clinical effect

questions.explanation: Dislocation of the lunate is produced by a fall on the acutely dorsiflexed hand with the elbow flexed; it displaces the lunate anteriorly, where it can compress the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, producing carpal tunnel syndrome-like features.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones, Clinical Anatomy

questions.question: In the long bones of the upper limb, the 'growing ends' (which fuse with the shaft latest) are located at which joints?

options.D: All joints fuse at exactly the same time

questions.explanation: By the law of ossification, the epiphysis that appears first at a given end fuses last. In the upper limb this means the upper end of the humerus and the lower ends of both the radius and ulna are the 'growing ends' — they fuse with their shafts later than the corresponding opposite ends.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Ossification

questions.question: Why is the metaphysis of a growing long bone especially important clinically when it lies partly within a joint capsule?

options.A: It has no blood supply, so infection cannot spread there at all
options.B: Being an actively growing, richly vascularised part of the bone, infection there can spread into the joint if the metaphysis is intracapsular (and vice versa)
options.C: It is always extracapsular in every long bone, so it never affects joints
options.D: It only matters in the lower limb, not the upper limb

questions.explanation: The metaphysis is the actively growing part of the bone adjacent to the epiphyseal line, with a rich blood supply — making it a common site for infection in young people. Where the metaphysis is partly or wholly intracapsular (as at the upper end of the humerus), joint infection can spread to the metaphysis, and metaphyseal disease can spread into the joint.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Capsular Attachments and Epiphyseal Lines

questions.question: Madelung's deformity results from retarded growth of which structure?

options.A: The lower end of the radius
options.B: The upper end of the humerus
options.C: The olecranon process of the ulna

questions.explanation: Madelung's deformity is a dorsal subluxation (displacement) of the lower end of the ulna, caused by retarded growth of the lower end of the radius.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy

questions.question: Which carpal bone is described as the largest, with a rounded head, occupying the centre of the distal row?
questions.explanation: The capitate is the largest carpal bone, identified by its rounded head, and sits in the distal row.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones

questions.question: The hook-like projection near the base of which carpal bone gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum?
questions.explanation: The hamate is wedge-shaped with a hook projecting from the distal part of its palmar surface; the tip of the hook gives attachment to the flexor retinaculum, and its medial side gives origin to flexor digiti minimi and opponens digiti minimi.

questions.question: The ulna is often described as the 'stabilising bone' of the forearm because:

options.A: Its trochlear notch grips the lower end of the humerus, giving the radius a stable foundation from which to pronate and supinate
options.B: It is the only bone that moves during pronation/supination
options.C: It bears the entire weight of the upper limb at the wrist joint
options.D: It has no muscular attachments, unlike the radius

questions.explanation: The ulna's trochlear notch grips the lower end of the humerus at the elbow, forming a stable hinge. This gives the radius the fixed foundation it needs to rotate around the ulna for efficient pronation and supination of the hand.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy

questions.question: After a fracture of both the radius and ulna shafts, why must cross-union (bony union between the two bones) be specifically prevented during healing?

options.B: Cross-union would permanently fuse the radius and ulna together, abolishing pronation and supination of the hand
options.C: Cross-union only affects elbow flexion, not the hand
options.D: It increases the risk of scaphoid fracture

questions.explanation: Pronation and supination depend on the radius being able to rotate around a stable ulna. If the two bones heal fused together (cross-union), that rotation becomes impossible, so surgeons take specific care during fixation of combined radius-ulna shaft fractures to prevent it.
